title: Chesterton's Fence: Before You Drop a Family Custom, Find Out Why It Was Built
topic: tư duy: hàng rào Chesterton và phong tục gia đình
unit: Chặng 1/12 · Ngôi nhà & gia đình Việt · Tuần 1/4: Gia đình, họ hàng & xưng hô
summary: G.K. Chesterton's parable of the fence (The Thing, 1929) says: do not remove something until you understand why it was put there. Applied to the death-anniversary meal, Tết taboos and the family register, the tool shows how to keep a custom's function while changing its form, when a custom deserves to go, and how asking 'what was this for?' works just as well in a reorganised office.
body:
Every family has customs that look pointless from the outside. Why must the eldest son's family host the death-anniversary meal (*đám giỗ*) even though the youngest daughter has the biggest house? Why does grandmother insist that nobody sweeps the floor on the first morning of Tết? Why do relatives keep a handwritten family register (*gia phả*) when everyone has a phone full of photos? A sharp young person, newly confident in her own judgment, is tempted to say: this makes no sense, let's drop it.

This piece offers a thinking tool for exactly that moment. It is called **Chesterton's fence**, and its message is not "never change anything". It is: *before you remove something, find out why it was put there.*

## The parable

In 1929 the English writer G.K. Chesterton published a book of essays called *The Thing*. In a chapter titled "The Drift from Domesticity" he opens with a line that has become famous: "In the matter of reforming things, as distinct from deforming them, there is one plain and simple principle".

He then describes a fence or gate built across a road. A modern-minded reformer arrives, sees no use for it, and proposes to clear it away. A wiser reformer answers him, roughly: if you don't see the use of it, I certainly won't let you clear it away. "Go away and think." Come back when you can tell me what it was for, and then I may let you remove it.

The point is subtle. The wiser reformer is not defending the fence. He is defending the *order of operations*: understand first, decide second. Fences, Chesterton argues, are not built by sleepwalkers or lunatics. Somebody spent effort putting it there, which means somebody once had a reason. The reason may be outdated, or even foolish, but you cannot know that until you have found it.

## Why our minds skip this step

Chesterton's fence works because it pushes against a habit we all share. When we look at a custom, we see its **costs** immediately (time, money, inconvenience) but its **benefits** are often invisible, because they show up as problems that *didn't* happen.

This is where last week's and this week's tools meet. In the language of systems thinking, many customs are **balancing feedback loops**: quiet mechanisms that keep a system steady. You notice a balancing loop mainly when it breaks. And in the language of Kahneman's two systems, the fast mind (System 1) answers "Is this useful?" by asking an easier question: "Can I see what it does right now?" If the answer is no, it jumps to "useless". The fence asks you to hand the question to the slow mind (System 2).

## Applying the fence to family customs

Let's go back to the three examples and do the homework the wiser reformer demands.

### The death-anniversary meal at the eldest son's house

On the surface: an inconvenient tradition that makes one household carry the burden. Look for the reason, though, and several functions appear. The *đám giỗ* is a fixed date that pulls a scattered family into one room at least once a year. Hosting it at the house of the eldest line (*trưởng*) keeps one clear "home base" for the lineage, so nobody has to negotiate every year whose turn it is, which is exactly the kind of argument that splits siblings. The altar and the inheritance of the ancestral home (*hương hỏa*) are tied together, as we saw in Thursday's piece on inheritance. The custom is, in part, a coordination device.

Knowing this changes the conversation. If the eldest brother's flat is genuinely too small, the family can keep the *function* (one fixed gathering, one recognised host line) while changing the *form* (rent a room, cook at the youngest sister's house but let the eldest brother lead the offering). That is reform. Simply declaring "the tradition is outdated" and letting each branch do its own thing is, in Chesterton's word, deforming.

### No sweeping on the first morning of Tết

The stated reason is spiritual: sweeping on New Year's morning "sweeps away luck". You do not have to share the belief to see other functions. The house has already been cleaned thoroughly before Tết, so a ban on chores gives the people who usually do them (very often women) a morning off. It also marks the first day as different from ordinary days. Once you see this, you may decide to keep the custom for your mother's sake even if you don't believe in the luck, or you may decide it is harmless either way. What you will not do is lecture her about superstition at the breakfast table, which wins the argument and loses the morning.

### The handwritten family register

Why keep a *gia phả* in a digital age? Because it was never only a list of names. It records who belongs to which branch, which generation each person is in, and therefore how people should address one another, as Tuesday's piece on lineages showed. It records death-anniversary dates. It is also an object: kept by the head of the lineage, brought out at gatherings, a symbol of continuity. A family that wants to digitise it might do so, but the fence suggests keeping the *role* of the register keeper and the ritual of updating it together, because those carry part of the value.

## The fence is not a wall

It is easy to misuse this idea as a defence of everything old. Chesterton's own framing protects against that: he is talking about *reforming* things, and the wise reformer does let the fence be removed once its purpose is understood. Shane Parrish's essay on the principle puts it plainly: "The point is not that the status quo is always right, that every fence should remain standing."

Sometimes you go and think, and you find that the original reason was bad. A preference for sons that leads to sex-selective abortion, for instance, was built on a lineage system in which only sons could carry on the ancestral worship. You now understand the fence completely, and understanding it is precisely what lets you argue against it well: you can address the real worry (who will tend the altar?) instead of mocking the people who hold it. Vietnam's laws have taken that path, banning sex selection while encouraging communities to write gender equality into their own village conventions (*hương ước*).

Other times you find that the reason was good once but circumstances have changed. Large households needed strict rules about who eats first because food was scarce; that need has largely gone, even if the gesture of inviting elders to eat first (*mời cơm*) survives as courtesy. Here, the fence lets you keep the courtesy and drop the scarcity logic.

So there are three possible outcomes of the homework:

1. **The reason still holds.** Keep the custom, perhaps with a lighter form.
2. **The reason has changed.** Keep the function, change the form.
3. **The reason was harmful.** Remove the custom, but replace whatever real need it served.

The only outcome Chesterton rules out is the fourth: remove it without knowing which of the first three applies.

## Using it at work

The same tool travels well to an office, especially a public one in the middle of a reorganisation. After Vietnam merged provinces and abolished the district level in 2025, many local offices inherited procedures, forms and habits from several predecessor bodies. Some will look redundant: a second signature, an extra logbook, a phone call to confirm what is already in the system.

Before proposing to cut one, ask the colleague who has been there longest: *"Chị ơi, cái sổ này ngày trước để làm gì ạ?"* ("What was this logbook originally for?"). Often the answer reveals a past incident: a lost file, a complaint, an audit finding. Sometimes the answer is "no idea, we've always done it", which is itself useful information: now you know nobody is relying on it consciously, and you can test removing it carefully. And asking first has a social bonus: it shows respect for the people who built the fence, which makes them far more willing to help you take it down if it turns out to be useless.

## How to practise

1. **Name the fence.** When you catch yourself thinking "this custom is pointless", write it down in one line.
2. **List three possible reasons** it exists, including at least one that is social (who does it bring together, who does it protect from arguments) and one that is practical.
3. **Ask an elder** what they think it is for. Listen for the story, not just the rule.
4. **Sort it** into one of the three outcomes above.
5. **Only then decide** what you would keep, change or drop, and how you would explain it to the person who cares about it most.

Done regularly, this habit makes you slower to scoff and quicker to understand, which, in a Vietnamese family or a Vietnamese office, is a large part of what people mean by being *ý tứ*: thoughtful, perceptive and considerate.

unsure: The functions suggested for each custom (coordination, rest for those who do chores, branch records) are interpretations offered for practice, not findings from a specific study; families may explain their customs differently.

connect.why: Many customs act as balancing feedback loops whose benefits are invisible until they break, which is why the fence asks you to look for them first.
The death-anniversary meal at the eldest line's house is tied to the ancestral-property arrangement (hương hỏa) described in Thursday's inheritance piece.
Judging a custom useless because you cannot see what it does is System 1 substituting an easier question; the fence hands the question to System 2.

check.q: In Chesterton's parable, what exactly does the wiser reformer object to: removing the fence, or something else?
check.a: He objects to removing it before understanding why it was built. Once the reformer can explain its purpose, the fence may be removed; the principle is about the order of understanding before deciding.

check.q: Why are the benefits of an old custom often harder to see than its costs?
check.a: Costs like time and money are visible now, while benefits often appear as problems that never happened, such as quarrels avoided or a family kept in touch. Such customs work like balancing loops that you notice only when they break.

check.q: Your office keeps a paper logbook that duplicates the electronic system. Using the fence, what should you do before proposing to drop it?
check.a: Ask long-serving colleagues what it was originally for and list possible reasons. Then sort it: keep it, keep the function in a new form, or remove it while covering any real need it served.

try: This week, pick one custom in your family or one routine at work that seems pointless. Write three possible reasons it exists, then ask an older relative or colleague what it was for, and note which of the three outcomes (keep, change the form, remove) it falls into.
